clauses.reason: Paragraph 1 designates the Under Secretary, then the ranking Assistant Secretary, then the Solicitor of the Department of the Interior to perform the duties of the Secretary of the Interior. Executive Order 10753 of February 15, 1958 ends with “This order supersedes Executive Order” and names Executive Order No. 10156 of August 26, 1950 by number, date and title, replacing the succession with a new one; no savings or exception clause appears. The first end is February 15, 1958.

Paragraph 2 says which Assistant Secretary is the ranking one for the purposes of paragraph 1(b). It has no operation once paragraph 1(b) is replaced, so it ends with paragraph 1 when Executive Order 10753, whose closing sentence is “This order supersedes Executive Order” naming Executive Order No. 10156, supersedes the order on February 15, 1958.

Paragraph 3 says the order supersedes Executive Order No. 9866 of June 14, 1947, which designated officers to act as Secretary of the Interior. Its supersession of that earlier order was performed when this order took effect on August 26, 1950, and Executive Order No. 9866 stays superseded as a surviving consequence. The held bytes for the signing-time end cannot be narrowed to the paragraph, so the first end recorded is the one a narrow held sentence supports: Executive Order 10753 of February 15, 1958 ends with “This order supersedes Executive Order” No. 10156 of August 26, 1950, which supersedes the whole order, paragraph 3 included, and has no exception. The earlier signing-time reading is disclosed and not adopted.

research_rationale:
Executive Order 10156 (15 FR 5789 (Federal Register of August 29, 1950)) was signed August 26, 1950. The held text begins with unrelated railroad-list pages of the same Federal Register issue and carries an unrelated sugar regulation after the order; the dossier's clause covered the railroad list's table fragments, so the inventory is corrected to the order's own text. The order designates, under section 179 of the Revised Statutes, the officers who perform the duties of the Secretary of the Interior in case of death, resignation, absence or sickness: the Under Secretary (1(a)), then the ranking Assistant Secretary (1(b)), then the Solicitor (1(c)); paragraph 2 defines the ranking Assistant Secretary; paragraph 3 supersedes Executive Order No. 9866 of June 14, 1947. On 2026-10-14 the designations in paragraphs 1 and 2 are terminated by Executive Order 10753 (23 FR 1107 (Federal Register of February 20, 1958)), signed February 15, 1958 by President Eisenhower, which sets a new order of succession and closes with the sentence “This order supersedes Executive Order” naming Executive Order No. 10156 of August 26, 1950 and its title. That sentence names this order by number and date and has no exception or saving clause. Paragraph 3 supersedes Executive Order No. 9866; that supersession was performed when the order took effect on August 26, 1950, which is disclosed as a candidate earlier end and not adopted, because the held bytes for it cannot be narrowed to the paragraph. The first end of paragraph 3, as of paragraphs 1 and 2, is the supersession of the whole order by Executive Order 10753 on 1958-02-15. The order has no own-terms sunset. The only later instrument in the held corpus that names the order is Executive Order 10753 (the neighbouring Federal Register page of Executive Order 10155 reprints this order's heading, not a later instrument). The Federal Register disposition-note search lists the one hit, Executive Order 10753; the eCFR citation search reports no hit. The packet's U.S. Code search entry reports no hit either, but the current-law table (jobs/current-law/output/ORDERS_CURRENT_LAW.csv) records two U.S. Code mentions of this order, both in the editorial notes to 43 U.S.C. 1451 (MENTIONS.csv rows usc:3aa65a4930ed and usc:639d9884e79e): the note for Executive Order No. 9866 says it was superseded by this order, effective August 26, 1950 (15 F.R. 5789), and the note for this order says it was superseded by Executive Order 10753, effective February 15, 1958 (23 F.R. 1107). Both notes agree with the dates recorded here and neither adds an earlier end. The superseded Executive Order No. 9866 stays superseded; that is a surviving consequence of paragraph 3 and not a command left to end.

savings.reason: The supersession of Executive Order No. 9866 in paragraph 3 is a performed act whose consequence survives (that earlier order stays superseded). The designations in paragraphs 1 and 2 left nothing accrued once Executive Order 10753 replaced them; neither the order nor Executive Order 10753 contains a saving clause for acts under the earlier designation.
